claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel carries a naturally formed native iron oxide layer.
Corrosion-related degradation of Q235 steel is governed by the integrity and thermal stability of its native oxide film.
At room temperature, a compact and adherent native oxide film suppresses further corrosion of Q235 steel.
At elevated temperatures, the native oxide film becomes porous or cracks and exposes the underlying Q235 steel to accelerated corrosion.
The native surface film on Q235 steel consists primarily of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 layers.
At lower temperatures, the oxide film limits access of oxygen and corrosive species to the underlying metal by acting as a passive barrier.
Thermal instability at elevated temperature induces cracking or porosity in the oxide film.
Cracking or porosity reduces passivation and enhances localized corrosion.
Chemically removing the native oxide and preventing its reformation will isolate the effect of oxide-film integrity.
At room temperature, intact-film coupons will have lower corrosion rates than oxide-removed coupons.
At elevated temperature, initially intact oxide films will develop cracking or porosity.
At elevated temperature, degradation of the initially intact film will accelerate corrosion relative to the untreated baseline.
At elevated temperature, oxide-removed coupons with inhibited oxide reformation will have even higher corrosion rates than initially intact-film coupons.
The proposed mechanism is most influential when corrosion is governed predominantly by oxygen and salt-ion diffusion through surface films.
The relevant thermal-instability range extends roughly from ambient temperature to 150°C.
Alloying elements other than iron are present only in trace amounts in Q235 steel and are not primary contributors in this study.
The protective role of native oxide films in corrosion is well known.
A correlation between elevated-temperature film degradation and increased metal loss would identify film integrity as the governing cause.

contradictions.description: The prediction says that samples with an initially intact oxide layer will show accelerated corrosion relative to the untreated baseline, but the baseline is itself untreated Q235 steel with the intact native oxide layer under identical conditions. These groups are not distinguishable as defined.

The predicted outcome ranks oxide-removed/inhibited samples as having even higher elevated-temperature corrosion than intact-film samples, whereas the falsification rule expects degradation of the intact oxide to correlate with accelerated corrosion relative to the treated samples.
